## Introduction and overview {#intro}

  ----------------------- -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Module                  Graph Machine and Deep Learning for Generative AI
  Code                    CSC_52072_EP
  Team and workload       Heads ("responsables" on the 2026–2027 sheet): Johannes Lutzeyer and Michalis Vazirgiannis (École Polytechnique); head of the scheduled X3A session: Johannes Lutzeyer · teaching team listed on the sheet: Guillaume Lachaud, Ye Zhu · teaching volume not displayed on the 2026–2027 sheet (36 h per the LLGA curriculum wiki, see the session plan · 4.5 ECTS) · from graph theory foundations to GNNs, graph generation and GraphRAG — the module that gives the master's program its name, and the foundation of the M2 module "Advanced Graph Neural Networks".
  Period                  Autumn semester · period 2 (from 04/01/2027 to 19/03/2027) · X3A session "Graph Machine and Deep Learning for Generative AI"; course taught in English
  Assessment              Quizzes and team projects (the course description); the LLGA section of the 2026–2027 sheet displays no assessment modality, resit rule or weighting
  Status in the program   [Mandatory]{.badge .mandatory}[Core of the master]{.badge .recommended}
  ----------------------- -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Audience**: an engineer who has already trained an MLP / CNN and wants to keep *structure* (fraud, molecules, KGs) instead of flattening it away.

**Empirical first**: a fraud model whose impressive test score came only from edges leaking across the train/test split; message passing that oversmooths after 4 layers — then we name GNNs, spectra, GraphRAG.

From graph-theory foundations to GNNs, generation and GraphRAG. Core module of the master: concepts reappear in M2 ([Advanced GNN](../m2-advanced-gnn/index.html), [LLMs](../m2-large-language-models/index.html)).

### What you will be able to do

-   Model an applied problem as a graph and identify the associated learning task (node, edge, or whole graph).
-   Explore a graph and compute its descriptive statistics (BFS distances, clustering, centralities).
-   Compare nodes and whole graphs with similarity measures and graph kernels (Weisfeiler-Lehman, random-walk).
-   Encode the structure of a graph into node embeddings usable by a classical model.
-   Understand spectral filters and spectral clustering via the graph Laplacian.
-   Build and train a GNN by message passing.
-   Diagnose heterophily and handle temporal graphs without leaking the future.
-   Build E(3)-invariant and equivariant models for geometric graphs (molecules, proteins).
-   Solve link prediction and use graph auto-encoders.
-   Scale a GNN to massive graphs (neighborhood sampling, mini-batches).
-   Generate realistic graphs with generative models.
-   Combine graphs and LLMs: GraphRAG and hybrid approaches.

### Official objectives and syllabus (2026-2027 catalog)

The official 2026–2027 sheet (X3A session of the same name, period X-3A-P2, from 04/01/2027 to 19/03/2027, taught in English) sets the objective of introducing students to graph networks and deep learning — their mathematical foundations, the design of architectures and their practical applications — a field it describes as especially important given the current volume of industrial and academic work.

The description announces machine- and deep-learning methods for graph-structured data, defined as an underlying graph with vector data observed on the nodes, the edges or both: fundamental descriptive statistics of graphs and probabilistic models that generate graphs, graph kernel methods, then a complete overview of deep learning on graphs, notably graph neural networks, closing with applications and a perspective on current challenges and future directions.

Assessment: quizzes and team projects (description; the LLGA section of the sheet displays no modality). Prerequisites: not displayed. Teaching volume: not displayed. The sheet lists a nine-lecture programme ("changes may occur during the semester"), matched below.

### Where this course fits in the program

**Mandatory** module of period 2 of M1 (teaching volume not displayed on the 2026–2027 sheet; 36 h and 4.5 ECTS per the LLGA curriculum wiki), of which Johannes Lutzeyer and Michalis Vazirgiannis are the official heads: it is the heart of the master's program, the one that structures the "graph" axis around which the advanced M2 modules are organized.

Official prerequisites: not displayed on the 2026–2027 sheet.

-   **Prerequisites** — [Machine Learning](../m1p1-machine-learning/index.html) and one Deep Learning course, taken either in P1 ([Deep Learning, ch. 6](../m1p1-deep-learning/index.html#ch6)) or in P2 ([Deep Learning P2, transformers](../m1p2-deep-learning-p2/index.html#dl-textgen)): attention is presented there and reused here. Students who take Deep Learning in P2 meet VAEs and diffusion after sessions 8 and 11 of this course, so ch. 6 and 9.5 recall what they need; the [Refresher Neural Nets](../m1p1-refresher-neural-nets/index.html) bridges the basics. Add the graph algorithms of the [Refresher in Computer Science](../m1p1-refresher-cs/index.html) (BFS, Dijkstra); the refresher section goes over the graph theory useful for the course.
-   **Downstream modules** — it is the direct foundation of [Advanced Graph Neural Networks](../m2-advanced-gnn/index.html) (M2) and [Graph Generative Models and Applications](../m2-graph-generative-models/index.html) (M2); its GraphRAG chapter prepares the [Large Language Models](../m2-large-language-models/index.html) module (M2), and it also feeds [Explainability, Security, Privacy of LLMs](../m2-explainability-security-privacy-llms/index.html) (M2).

### Course outline

-   **Refresher: graph theory** — vocabulary, spectra and random walks, then graph exploration (BFS, DFS, Dijkstra) and the descriptive statistics of a graph.
-   **Why graphs?** — the motivation: relational, non-Euclidean data, everywhere in industry and science.
-   **Learning tasks on graphs** — classifying a node, an edge, a whole graph: the taxonomy of the field; node similarity measures and graph kernels (Weisfeiler-Lehman, random walks).
-   **Node embeddings** — encoding structure into vectors, with the constraints that guide them.
-   **Spectral filters and spectral clustering** — the Laplacian, its eigenvalues, and the partition that follows.
-   **GNNs and message passing** — the central building block: propagating information along the edges, layer after layer; heterophilous and temporal graphs.
-   **Link prediction and graph auto-encoders** — predicting missing edges and compressing graphs.
-   **GNNs at scale** — training on graphs that fit neither in memory nor in a single batch.
-   **Applications and hands-on** — going from equations to libraries on real use cases; geometric graphs, equivariance and biomedicine; benchmarking and open challenges.
-   **Graph generation** — producing new and realistic graphs: the entry into relational generative AI.
-   **Graphs × LLMs: GraphRAG and the hybrid** — making a knowledge graph and a large language model cooperate.
-   **Research at DaSciM (Lutzeyer, Vazirgiannis)** — a tour of the research work of Lutzeyer and Vazirgiannis (self-study).
-   **Exercises** and **References** — systematic training and sources to go further.

### Session plan {#sessions}

The sheet does publish a nine-lecture programme, and the plan follows its order with two changes, both made so that no session relies on a notion taught later: the spectral lecture (official 6) comes before the GNN lecture (official 5), because the GCN layer is derived from the spectral filter (Derivation 5.2); and the introduction to graph generative AI (official 4) is taught after GNNs, because the deep generative models of ch. 9 use GNN encoders and denoisers.

### How to study this module

-   Redo the refresher section even if you "know" graphs: BFS and Dijkstra are covered again because the rest of the course relies on them without warning.
-   Implement a message passing from scratch on a small hand-drawn graph before using a library: it is ten lines that light up the whole field.
-   Follow the spectral thread: Laplacian, spectral clustering then GNNs are the same object in three costumes — this thread also prepares the M2 module on geometric data.
-   Visualize node embeddings (dimensionality reduction) to check your intuition on each dataset.
-   Read the GraphRAG chapter in parallel with the [Introduction to Text Mining and NLP](../m1p2-nlp-text-mining/index.html) module, taught in the same period: the two shed light on each other.
-   Redo the exercises of each section before moving on to the next; they build the foundation reused by all the downstream M2 modules.

::: note
[independent note]{.tag} The "graph" half of the master: GraphRAG (ch. 10) is the junction with the LLM axis, extended in M2 by Advanced GNN and LLMs. Fraud, recommendation, chemistry, enterprise KGs — cases where discarding structure costs more than a bad hyperparameter.
:::

## 0. Refresher: graph theory {#ch0}

Every later chapter manipulates the same few objects — the adjacency matrix, the degrees, the Laplacian, random walks — and uses their properties without stopping to prove them. This refresher states and proves those properties once, so that the walks of ch. 3 and the spectral arguments of ch. 4 rest on solid ground.

:::: recap
::: recap-title
L3 prerequisites — the "graph" object (cf. Refresher CS)
:::

-   **Definitions**: $G = (V, E)$; directed/undirected, weighted; degree $d_v$, neighbors $\mathcal{N}(v)$, adjacency matrix $A$, degree matrix $D = \mathrm{diag}(d_v)$. Paths, connectivity, components, cycles, DAGs.
-   **Euler and Königsberg (1736)**: crossing the 7 bridges is impossible because more than two vertices have odd degree — the first theorem of graph theory; the abstraction (nodes + edges) founded the discipline.
-   **Linear algebra**: $(A^k)_{ij}$ counts the walks of length $k$ from $i$ to $j$ (vertices may repeat); eigenvalues of $A$ = spectrum of the graph; symmetric matrices diagonalizable in an orthonormal basis (algebra reminder).
-   **Stochastic matrices**: $P = D^{-1}A$ = random walk; stationary distribution, PageRank $\pi \propto (I - \alpha P)^{-1}\mathbf{1}$.
::::

::: def
[Definition 0.1 — Isomorphism, automorphism, subgraph]{.tag} Two graphs $G = (V, E)$ and $G' = (V', E')$ are **isomorphic** if there exists a bijection $\pi : V \to V'$ such that
$$
(u, v) \in E \iff (\pi(u), \pi(v)) \in E'.
$$

An **automorphism** is an isomorphism of $G$ onto itself; their set forms a group $\mathrm{Aut}(G)$. A **subgraph** of $G$ is formed of $S \subseteq V$ and a subset of $E \cap (S \times S)$; the *induced* subgraph keeps all the internal edges.

Deciding isomorphism is a problem known neither NP-complete nor polynomial; the **Weisfeiler-Lehman** test (Algorithm 2.5; [Advanced GNN, ch. 2](../m2-advanced-gnn/index.html#ch2) in M2) is its fundamental heuristic — and the expressivity bound of GNNs.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.2 — Connectivity and shortest paths]{.tag} The relation "$u \sim v$ if there exists a path from $u$ to $v$" is an equivalence relation; its classes are the connected components. Between two vertices of the same component, every path of minimal length (shortest path) is a simple path (without repeated vertex).

::: proof
Reflexivity (path of length 0), symmetry (undirected graph: reverse the path) and transitivity (concatenate) are immediate. If a path from $u$ to $v$ visits a vertex $w$ twice, we delete the cycle between the two visits: the path strictly shortens. A path of minimal length therefore cannot contain a cycle, so every vertex appears there only once: it is simple, of length $\leq n - 1$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 0.3 (spectral theorem) and counting by the trace]{.tag} Every real symmetric matrix $S \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ writes $S = U \Lambda U^\top$ with $U$ orthogonal and $\Lambda$ real diagonal.

For the adjacency of a simple graph, three counting identities follow:
$$
\mathrm{tr}(A) = 0, \qquad \mathrm{tr}(A^2) = 2|E|, \qquad \mathrm{tr}(A^3) = 6\,|\{\text{triangles}\}|.
$$

::: proof
$\mathrm{tr}(A^2) = \sum_i (A^2)_{ii} = \sum_i d_i$, each edge contributing to two degrees.

$(A^3)_{ii}$ counts the closed walks of length 3 through $i$: these are exactly the triangles containing $i$, each traversed in both directions from $i$. Each triangle $\{i, j, k\}$ thus produces 2 closed walks for each of its 3 vertices, i.e. 6 countings.

Conversely a closed walk of length 3 $i \to j \to k \to i$ visits three pairwise distinct, pairwise adjacent vertices. [∎]{.qed}
:::

Immediate application in learning: counting triangles (motifs) by matrix products — the basic ingredient of the structural features of ch. 9 and of the expressivity theory of [Advanced GNN, ch. 2](../m2-advanced-gnn/index.html#ch2).
::::

:::: def
[Definition 0.4 — The Laplacian of a graph]{.tag}
$$
L = D - A, \qquad \text{or normalized: } L_{\mathrm{sym}} = I - D^{-1/2} A\, D^{-1/2}.
$$
For every vector $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ ($n = |V|$):

::: key
[Key result — the Laplacian quadratic form]{.tag}
$$
x^\top L x = \sum_{(u,v) \in E} (x_u - x_v)^2 \ \geq\ 0
$$
:::

— $L$ is positive semi-definite; its eigenvalues $0 = \lambda_1 \leq \lambda_2 \leq \dots \leq \lambda_n$ encode connectivity.

$\lambda_2$ (the *spectral gap*, Fiedler 1973) measures the difficulty of cutting the graph, and the number of zero eigenvalues equals the number of connected components.

::: proof
$x^\top D x = \sum_v d_v x_v^2$ and $x^\top A x = 2 \sum_{(u,v) \in E} x_u x_v$ (symmetric matrix); hence
$$
x^\top L x = \sum_{(u,v) \in E} (x_u^2 + x_v^2 - 2 x_u x_v).
$$

For the multiplicity of 0: reordering the vertices by components makes $A$ (and $L$) block-diagonal; each block $L_C$ has the indicator $\mathbf{1}_C$ as kernel, since $x^\top L_C x = 0$ forces $x$ constant on each connected component (the sum of squares cancels edge by edge, and connectivity propagates the constant — Prop. 0.2). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 0.5 — The spectrum tells the story]{.tag}

-   Path of $n$ vertices: $\lambda_k = 2(1 - \cos\frac{k\pi}{n})$, $k = 0, \dots, n-1$;
-   complete graph: $0$ then $n$ (multiplicity $n-1$);
-   cycle of $n$ vertices: $\lambda_k = 2(1 - \cos\frac{2k\pi}{n})$, $k = 0, \dots, n-1$.

A "two-community" graph has a small $\lambda_2$; the Fiedler eigenvector separates the communities — this is the heart of **spectral clustering**, developed in ch. 4 (direct bridge with the PCA of the Machine Learning module).
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.6 — Random walks: stationarity and ergodicity]{.tag} Let $G$ be connected undirected, $P = D^{-1}A$, $m = |E|$. The distribution $\pi_v = d_v / (2m)$ is stationary: $\pi^\top P = \pi^\top$.

If moreover $G$ is not bipartite, the chain is irreducible and aperiodic, hence **ergodic**:
$$
P^t(x, \cdot) \xrightarrow[t \to \infty]{} \pi \qquad \text{whatever the starting point } x.
$$

::: proof
*Detailed balance*:
$$
\pi_u P_{uv} = \frac{d_u}{2m} \cdot \frac{\mathbb{1}[(u,v) \in E]}{d_u} = \frac{\mathbb{1}[(u,v) \in E]}{2m},
$$
a quantity symmetric in $u, v$; summing over $u$, $(\pi^\top P)_v = \pi_v$.

*Irreducibility*: connectivity makes every vertex reachable.

*Periodicity*: on a bipartite graph, every closed walk has even length ($P^t(x, x) = 0$ for odd $t$), so the chain has period 2.

Conversely, a connected non-bipartite graph contains a cycle of odd length $\ell$. From any vertex $x$ the walk can come back in 2 steps (along an edge and back) or in an odd number of steps (walk $k$ steps to the cycle, go around it, walk back: $2k + \ell$ steps), and $\gcd(2, 2k + \ell) = 1$ — period 1.

The convergence theorem for finite irreducible aperiodic Markov chains ([Reinforcement Learning, ch. 0, Theorem 0.2](../m1p2-reinforcement-learning/index.html#ch0), session 1 of the same period) concludes. [∎]{.qed}
:::

Practical consequence: the walks of DeepWalk (ch. 3) "mix" the distribution toward $\pi \propto$ degrees — hence the bias of embeddings toward hubs, partly corrected by node2vec and by NetMF.
::::

::: def
[Definition 0.7 — Modularity (Newman & Girvan, 2004)]{.tag} For a partition $\mathcal{C} = \{C_1, \dots, C_k\}$ of the vertices:
$$
Q(\mathcal{C}) = \frac{1}{2m} \sum_{i,j} \Big[ A_{ij} - \frac{d_i\, d_j}{2m} \Big]\, \delta(c_i, c_j),
$$
where $c_i$ is the community of $i$ and $\delta$ the indicator.

$Q$ compares the *observed* density of intra-community edges to the *expected* one under the configuration model (edges redistributed while preserving degrees, term $d_i d_j / 2m$).

*Maximization sketch*: maximizing $Q$ exactly is NP-hard; Louvain does it greedily. Each node $i$ in turn moves to the neighboring community $C$ that most increases the modularity — the gain of moving an isolated node $i$ into $C$ is
$$
\Delta Q = \frac{k_{i,C}}{m} - \frac{\Sigma_C\, d_i}{2m^2},
$$
with $k_{i,C}$ the number of edges from $i$ to $C$ and $\Sigma_C$ the sum of the degrees in $C$. Then each community is contracted into a single node and the procedure restarts; hence hierarchies of communities used as-is by GraphRAG (ch. 10).

Known limit: resolution (Fortunato & Barthélemy, 2007). Two communities joined by a single edge are merged by modularity maximization as soon as each has fewer than about $\sqrt{m/2}$ internal edges, even when both are cliques.

Read the other way: a community found with fewer than about $\sqrt{2m}$ internal edges may hide smaller ones and should be inspected. The SBM (ch. 9) offers a better-founded statistical alternative.
:::

### Exploring and describing a graph

The second lecture of the official programme covers graph exploration and traditional graph algorithms, and the course description opens with the fundamental *descriptive statistics* of graphs. Before any learning, these are the first things computed on a new graph: they reveal its scale, its hubs and its local density, and they remain strong hand-crafted features for classical models.

:::: thm
[Algorithm 0.8 — Breadth-first search and unweighted shortest paths]{.tag} From a source $s$:

1.  set $\mathrm{dist}(s) = 0$, put $s$ in a FIFO queue;
2.  repeatedly pop a vertex $v$ and, for every neighbor $u$ not yet discovered, set $\mathrm{dist}(u) = \mathrm{dist}(v) + 1$, $\mathrm{parent}(u) = v$, and push $u$.

Cost $\mathcal{O}(|V| + |E|)$: each vertex is pushed once, each edge examined twice.

**Claim**: $\mathrm{dist}(u)$ is the length of a shortest path from $s$ to $u$, and the parent pointers form a shortest-path tree.

::: proof
The queue always holds vertices whose $\mathrm{dist}$ values are non-decreasing and differ by at most $1$ (true at the start; popping $v$ and pushing vertices with $\mathrm{dist}(v) + 1$ preserves it). Hence vertices are popped in non-decreasing order of $\mathrm{dist}$.

Suppose some vertex $u$ gets $\mathrm{dist}(u) > \delta(u)$, the true distance, and take such a $u$ with smallest $\delta(u)$. 

Let $w$ be its predecessor on a shortest path, so $\delta(w) = \delta(u) - 1$ and $\mathrm{dist}(w) = \delta(w)$ by minimality.

When $w$ was popped, $u$ was either undiscovered — then it received $\mathrm{dist}(w) + 1 = \delta(u)$, a contradiction.

Or it was already discovered from a vertex popped before $w$, whose $\mathrm{dist}$ is $\leq \mathrm{dist}(w)$, giving $\mathrm{dist}(u) \leq \delta(u)$, again a contradiction.

Conversely $\mathrm{dist}(u) \geq \delta(u)$ always, since the parent pointers trace an actual path of that length. [∎]{.qed}
:::

Replacing the queue by a stack gives **depth-first search**, used for connected components, cycle detection and topological order (DAGs); with non-negative edge weights, **Dijkstra**'s algorithm replaces the queue by a priority queue on tentative distances, in $\mathcal{O}((|V| + |E|)\log |V|)$. All three are recalled in the Refresher in Computer Science; here they are the primitives of the statistics below and of the neighborhood sampling of ch. 7.
::::

::: def
[Definition 0.9 — Descriptive statistics and centralities]{.tag} With $n = |V|$, $m = |E|$:

-   **degrees**: mean degree $2m/n$, density $2m / (n(n-1))$, and the degree distribution $p_k$ — often heavy-tailed in real networks ($p_k \propto k^{-\gamma}$ over a range of $k$), which produces hubs;
-   **clustering**: the local coefficient
    $$
    C_v = \frac{|\{\text{edges among the neighbors of } v\}|}{\binom{d_v}{2}} = \frac{(A^3)_{vv}}{d_v(d_v - 1)}
    $$
    (Theorem 0.3), and the global *transitivity*
    $$
    3 \times \#\text{triangles} / \#\text{connected triples};
    $$
-   **distances**: eccentricity of $v$ (largest BFS distance), diameter (largest eccentricity), average shortest-path length; a *small world* combines short paths with high clustering (Watts & Strogatz, 1998);
-   **centralities**:
    -   degree;
    -   *closeness* $c(v) = (n-1) / \sum_{u} \mathrm{dist}(v, u)$;
    -   *betweenness*
        $$
        b(v) = \sum_{s \neq v \neq t} \sigma_{st}(v)/\sigma_{st},
        $$
        where $\sigma_{st}$ counts the shortest $s$–$t$ paths and $\sigma_{st}(v)$ those through $v$ (Brandes' algorithm computes all of them in $\mathcal{O}(nm)$);
    -   *eigenvector* centrality $Ax = \lambda_1 x$;
    -   *PageRank*, the stationary law of the walk of Proposition 0.6 with teleportation:
        $$
        \pi^\top = \alpha\, \pi^\top P + (1 - \alpha)\,\mathbf{1}^\top / n;
        $$
-   **assortativity**: the correlation between the degrees at the two ends of an edge (social networks: positive; technological and biological networks: often negative).

These numbers are the classical features of node and graph classification, and the statistics compared by the MMD evaluation of generated graphs (9.6).
:::

::: ex
[Example 0.10 — The statistics of a small graph, computed]{.tag} Take the "kite" with vertices $a, b, c, d, e$ and edges $ab, ac, bc, cd, de$ (a triangle $abc$ with a tail $c - d - e$).

Here $n = m = 5$, density $5/10 = 0.5$, degrees $(2, 2, 3, 2, 1)$.

-   **BFS from $a$**: layers $\{a\}, \{b, c\}, \{d\}, \{e\}$, so the eccentricity of $a$ is $3$, which is also the diameter.
-   **Clustering**: $C_a = C_b = 1$; $C_c = 1/3$ (among its neighbors $a, b, d$ only $ab$ is an edge); $C_d = 0$; $C_e = 0$ by convention.

    One triangle and $\sum_v \binom{d_v}{2} = 1 + 1 + 3 + 1 + 0 = 6$ connected triples give a transitivity $3/6 = 0.5$.
-   **Closeness**: the distances from $c$ sum to $1 + 1 + 1 + 2 = 5$, so $c(c) = 4/5 = 0.8$.

    From $d$: $6$, so $c(d) \approx 0.67$; from $a$: $7$, so $c(a) \approx 0.57$.
-   **Betweenness** (unordered pairs): every shortest path from $\{a, b\}$ to $\{d, e\}$ passes through $c$, so $b(c) = 4$.

    The paths from $\{a, b, c\}$ to $e$ pass through $d$, so $b(d) = 3$; $b(a) = b(b) = b(e) = 0$.

Vertex $c$ has only one more edge than the others, but it controls all traffic between the two halves — what degree alone does not show.
:::

## 1. Why graphs? {#ch1}

Concrete scene: fraud detection on a transaction graph (nodes = accounts, edges = transfers). A tabular classifier on account features hits 0.71 AUC; the same model enriched with a 2-hop neighborhood reaches 0.89 — until a random split leaks train↔test edges and inflates the score. This chapter states why structure matters, before writing a GNN.

::: note
[What breaks]{.tag} Treating nodes as i.i.d. (signal lost); splitting without blocking edges (leakage); stacking GCN layers until every embedding looks the same (over-smoothing). All three sabotage a GraphRAG as much as a toy Karate Club.
:::

Real-world data is *relational*: the structure carries information that i.i.d. methods ignore.

Social networks (friendships), molecules (bonds), transaction networks (fraud!), enterprise knowledge graphs (customers, products, processes), computer networks, citation clusters, legal ontologies… All are naturally graphs, often **heterogeneous** (typed nodes/edges: "buys", "owns", "works with") and **dynamic** (timestamped edges: transactions second by second).

Also typically: *few labels* (a few dozen annotated nodes out of millions) — the semi-supervised regime of ch. 5 — and distributions *biased by sampling* (the observed edges are not a uniform sample of the interactions).

::: note
[independent note]{.tag} LLMs excel at text but struggle with: *structured relations*, *factual fidelity* (hallucinations), and non-textual data. Graphs fill exactly these gaps:

-   **GraphRAG**: connecting the LLM to structured proprietary data — today the most effective approach for making an LLM reliable in the enterprise (ch. 10);
-   **GNN + LLM**: generative AI on structured data (generating molecules, plans, recommendations);
-   **Industrial applications**: pharma/biotech (molecules = graphs), finance (transaction networks, systemic risk), recommendation, supply chain, multi-agent systems (agent workflows are DAGs — RL module).
:::

::: note
[Common thread of the master's program]{.tag} Three places of the graph in generative AI: *inside* the model (the attention of transformers is a complete dynamic graph — Deep Learning module), *for* the model (GraphRAG, structural encoding — ch. 10), *between* models (agent orchestration = DAG programming). This module lays the foundations of all three; the M2 module "Advanced GNN" extends each one.
:::

## 2. Learning tasks on graphs {#ch2}

Before choosing a model, one must say *what* is predicted: a label per node, a score per pair of nodes, or a property of the whole graph. This chapter fixes that taxonomy, then the two constraints that every later model must respect: the symmetry under renumbering of the nodes, and the distinction between predicting on the training graph and on new graphs.

  Level       Task                                Examples
  ----------- ----------------------------------- -----------------------------------------------------------------
  node        node classification / regression    labeling an article (topic), detecting a fraudulent user
  link        link prediction                     recommendation, knowledge graph completion (ch. 6)
  graph       graph classification / regression   property of a molecule (toxic?), performance prediction
  graph       graph **generation**                molecule design, networks, synthetic graphs (ch. 9)
  structure   community clustering                segmentation, anomaly detection (modularity, ch. 0; SBM, ch. 9)

::: def
[Definition 2.1 — Permutation invariance and equivariance]{.tag} A graph has *neither a fixed size nor a canonical order of the nodes*: the model must be **permutation-invariant** (graph output) or **permutation-equivariant** (per-node output): for every permutation matrix $P$,
$$
f(P X, P A P^\top) = f(X, A) \quad \text{(invariant)}, \qquad f(PX, PAP^\top) = P f(X, A) \quad \text{(equivariant)}.
$$

CNNs (grid), RNNs (sequence) violate these constraints — hence dedicated architectures (ch. 5) and the whole expressivity theory of [Advanced GNN, ch. 2](../m2-advanced-gnn/index.html#ch2).
:::

::: note
[Transductive vs inductive — a distinction that structures the whole module]{.tag}

-   **Transductive**: training and testing on the *same* graph (embeddings ch. 3); impossible to predict for a node arriving after training;
-   **Inductive**: the model (its weights) reapplies to new graphs (GraphSAGE, GNNs ch. 5) — indispensable in production;
-   **Structural semi-supervised**: on Cora (2,708 nodes), 140 labels suffice — the structure relays the information (homophily hypothesis: neighbors share the label; when it fails, one needs "virtual" edges or heterophilous models — ch. 5, "Heterophily").
:::

### Similarity measures and graph kernels

The third lecture of the official programme is devoted to graph kernels and similarity measures — the way graphs were learned on before neural networks, and still the strongest baselines on many small benchmarks. Two questions are asked: how similar are two *nodes* of one graph (the basis of link prediction, ch. 6), and how similar are two *whole graphs* of different sizes, without any correspondence between their nodes (the basis of graph classification with kernel machines).

::: def
[Definition 2.2 — Node similarity measures]{.tag} For nodes $u, v$ with neighborhoods $\mathcal{N}(u), \mathcal{N}(v)$:

-   **common neighbors** $|\mathcal{N}(u) \cap \mathcal{N}(v)| = (A^2)_{uv}$;
-   **Jaccard**
    $$
    \frac{|\mathcal{N}(u) \cap \mathcal{N}(v)|}{|\mathcal{N}(u) \cup \mathcal{N}(v)|};
    $$
-   **Adamic-Adar** (a shared neighbor counts more if it is not a hub)
    $$
    \sum_{w \in \mathcal{N}(u) \cap \mathcal{N}(v)} \frac{1}{\log d_w};
    $$
-   **Katz** $S = \sum_{k \geq 1} \beta^k A^k = (I - \beta A)^{-1} - I$, which counts all walks between $u$ and $v$ with a weight decaying with length and converges for $\beta < 1/\lambda_{\max}(A)$;
-   **personalized PageRank** from $u$, evaluated at $v$.

The first three are *local* (two hops), the last two *global*.

In the kite of Example 0.10, $a$ and $d$ share the neighbor $c$ ($\mathcal{N}(a) = \{b, c\}$, $\mathcal{N}(d) = \{c, e\}$).

Common neighbors $1$, Jaccard $1/3$, Adamic-Adar $1/\log 3 \approx 0.91$.

These heuristics are the baselines any learned link predictor (ch. 6) must beat (Liben-Nowell & Kleinberg, 2007).
:::

::: def
[Definition 2.3 — Graph kernel]{.tag} A **graph kernel** is a function
$$
k(G, G') = \langle \varphi(G), \varphi(G') \rangle_{\mathcal{H}}
$$
for some feature map $\varphi$ into a Hilbert space — equivalently, a symmetric function whose Gram matrix on any finite set of graphs is positive semi-definite — and which is invariant under isomorphism.

Any kernel method of the Machine Learning module (SVM, kernel ridge regression, kernel PCA) then applies to a dataset of graphs of different sizes.

A *complete* kernel ($\varphi$ injective on isomorphism classes) would decide graph isomorphism, so computing one is at least as hard as that problem (Gärtner et al., 2003); practical kernels therefore compare *substructures* (R-convolution, Haussler, 1999):
$$
k(G, G') = \sum_{s \in S(G)} \sum_{s' \in S(G')} \kappa(s, s').
$$

Main families: **graphlet** kernels (histograms of the induced subgraphs on 3–5 vertices), **shortest-path** kernels (compare the multisets of shortest-path lengths, with end labels), **random-walk** kernels and **Weisfeiler-Lehman** kernels, detailed below.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.4 — The random-walk kernel through the product graph]{.tag} The **direct product graph** $G_\times$ of $G$ and $G'$ has the vertex pairs $(v, v')$ as nodes.

It has an edge between $(u, u')$ and $(v, v')$ iff $(u, v) \in E$ and $(u', v') \in E'$; for unlabeled graphs its adjacency is the Kronecker product $A_\times = A \otimes A'$.

The geometric random-walk kernel counts pairs of walks of equal length, with weight $\lambda^k$ for length $k$:
$$
k_{\mathrm{RW}}(G, G') = \sum_{k \geq 0} \lambda^k\, \mathbf{1}^\top A_\times^k\, \mathbf{1} = \mathbf{1}^\top (I - \lambda A_\times)^{-1}\, \mathbf{1}, \qquad \lambda < 1/\lambda_{\max}(A_\times).
$$
It is a valid kernel; for unlabeled graphs it reduces to $\sum_k \lambda^k\, w_k(G)\, w_k(G')$ with $w_k(G) = \mathbf{1}^\top A^k \mathbf{1}$ the number of walks of length $k$.

::: proof
By the mixed-product rule of Kronecker products, $(A \otimes A')^k = A^k \otimes A'^k$, so
$$
(A_\times^k)_{(u,u'),(v,v')} = (A^k)_{uv}\,(A'^k)_{u'v'}:
$$
a walk of length $k$ in $G_\times$ is exactly a pair of walks of length $k$, one in each graph.

Summing over all start and end pairs,
$$
\mathbf{1}^\top A_\times^k \mathbf{1} = (\mathbf{1}^\top A^k \mathbf{1})(\mathbf{1}^\top A'^k \mathbf{1}) = w_k(G)\, w_k(G').
$$
Hence
$$
k_{\mathrm{RW}} = \sum_k \lambda^k w_k(G) w_k(G') = \langle \varphi(G), \varphi(G') \rangle, \qquad \varphi(G) = (\lambda^{k/2} w_k(G))_{k \geq 0}
$$
— an inner product, so positive semi-definite.

The geometric series converges when $\lambda\, \lambda_{\max}(A_\times) < 1$, and then equals the matrix inverse. [∎]{.qed}
:::

Cost: a naive inversion of the $nn' \times nn'$ system takes $\mathcal{O}(n^6)$; Sylvester-equation and conjugate-gradient methods bring it to about $\mathcal{O}(n^3)$ (Vishwanathan et al., 2010). Weakness: walks may *totter* back and forth along one edge, which inflates similarity between unrelated graphs.
::::

::: thm
[Algorithm 2.5 — Weisfeiler-Lehman subtree kernel (Shervashidze et al., 2011)]{.tag} Start from labels $\ell_0(v)$ (node labels, or a constant). At iteration $h = 1, \dots, H$, give each node the new label
$$
\ell_h(v) = \mathrm{relabel}\Big(\ell_{h-1}(v),\ \{\!\{\ell_{h-1}(u) : u \in \mathcal{N}(v)\}\!\}\Big),
$$
where $\{\!\{\cdot\}\!\}$ is a multiset and $\mathrm{relabel}$ is an injective dictionary *shared by all the graphs of the dataset*.

Let $\varphi_h(G)$ count how many nodes carry each label at iteration $h$; the kernel is
$$
k_{\mathrm{WL}}(G, G') = \sum_{h=0}^{H} \langle \varphi_h(G), \varphi_h(G') \rangle .
$$

The label $\ell_h(v)$ encodes the rooted subtree of depth $h$ obtained by unfolding the neighborhood of $v$; computing all features costs $\mathcal{O}(H\,m)$ per graph — linear, which makes the WL kernel usable on thousands of graphs.

It is the *1-WL isomorphism test* (Definition 0.1) turned into features; message passing (ch. 5) is the same iteration with a learned, continuous relabeling, which is why GNNs are at most as discriminating as 1-WL ([Advanced GNN, ch. 2](../m2-advanced-gnn/index.html#ch2)).
:::

::: ex
[Example 2.6 — Two WL iterations, computed]{.tag} Compare the path $G_1 = 1{-}2{-}3{-}4$ and the star $G_2$ (center $0$, leaves $1, 2, 3$): both have 4 nodes and 3 edges. Start with a constant label $\circ$.

1.  **$h = 0$**: both histograms are $\{\circ : 4\}$, contribution $16$.
2.  **$h = 1$**: a node with one neighbor gets $A = (\circ, \{\circ\})$, two neighbors $B = (\circ, \{\circ, \circ\})$, three $C$.

    $G_1$: $\{A : 2, B : 2\}$; $G_2$: $\{A : 3, C : 1\}$; contribution $2 \cdot 3 = 6$.
3.  **$h = 2$**: in $G_1$ the ends become $D = (A, \{B\})$ and the inner nodes $E = (B, \{A, B\})$.

    In $G_2$ the center becomes $F = (C, \{A, A, A\})$ and the leaves $G = (A, \{C\})$; no label is shared, contribution $0$.

So $k_{\mathrm{WL}}(G_1, G_2) = 22$, while
$$
k(G_1, G_1) = 16 + 8 + 8 = 32, \qquad k(G_2, G_2) = 16 + 10 + 10 = 36;
$$
the normalized kernel is
$$
22/\sqrt{32 \cdot 36} \approx 0.65 .
$$

Limit: on regular graphs all labels stay equal — two disjoint triangles and the 6-cycle get identical WL features, although they are not isomorphic.
:::

::: note
[Kernels or GNNs?]{.tag} A kernel fixes the features ($\varphi$) and learns only the classifier; a GNN learns the features too, and uses continuous node attributes naturally.

On small graph-classification datasets (MUTAG, PROTEINS, NCI1), the WL kernel with an SVM remains a strong baseline (survey by Kriege, Johansson & Morris, 2020), and under a fair protocol even structure-agnostic baselines are hard for GNNs to beat (Errica et al., 2020); kernels lose ground on large datasets, continuous features and node-level tasks.

The node similarities above also reappear inside learned models: the shared-neighbor counts of $A^2$ are the structural features added to GNN link predictors (for example SEAL, Zhang & Chen, 2018).
:::

## 3. Node embeddings {#ch3}

A classical model (logistic regression, k-means) needs one vector per node, but a graph only gives relations. Node embeddings solve this by learning a vector $z_v \in \mathbb{R}^d$ for each node from the structure alone, so that nodes close in the graph get close vectors.

::: def
[Objective]{.tag} Learn $z_v \in \mathbb{R}^d$ such that *the similarity of the embeddings reflects proximity in the graph*: $\mathrm{sim}(z_u, z_v) \approx P(u \text{ neighbor of } v)$ — an implicit *factorization* of the adjacency matrix (or of a matrix of derived proximities), in contrast with the GNNs of ch. 5 which *condition* the embedding on the features $X$.
:::

::: thm
[DeepWalk (Perozzi et al., 2014) and node2vec (Grover & Leskovec, 2016)]{.tag}

1.  generate **random walks** from each node (length $\ell$, $r$ walks per node); node2vec biases the walk with $(p, q)$ — developed below;
2.  apply **word2vec skip-gram** to the walks: the "sentences" are sequences of nodes, the window $b$ defines the (center, context) pairs;
3.  afterwards: any vector method (k-means, classification…).

The random walk defines *proximity*: two often co-visited nodes get close embeddings — the **NetMF** theory (Qiu et al., 2018) shows retrospectively that DeepWalk *factorizes* a deterministic matrix of walks (Theorem 3.3).
:::

::: prop
[Derivation 3.1 — Skip-gram with negative sampling: the loss and its gradient]{.tag} For a (center $c$, context $o$) pair and $K$ negatives $v_1, \dots, v_K$ drawn from a noise distribution $P_n$ (unigram law raised to the power 3/4). This derivation is the site's reference for skip-gram; [NLP, ch. 4](../m1p2-nlp-text-mining/index.html#ch4), in the same period, builds on it with subsampling, GloVe and the shifted-PMI reading:
$$
\mathcal{L}(c, o) = -\log \sigma(z_o^\top z_c) \; - \; \sum_{k=1}^{K} \log \sigma(-z_{v_k}^\top z_c),
$$
with $\sigma(s) = 1/(1 + e^{-s})$.

Writing $s_k = z_{v_k}^\top z_c$ and differentiating $\frac{d}{ds}[-\log\sigma(s)] = \sigma(s) - 1$:
$$
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial z_c} = \big(\sigma(z_o^\top z_c) - 1\big)\, z_o \; + \; \sum_{k=1}^K \sigma(s_k)\, z_{v_k}, \qquad \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial z_o} = \big(\sigma(z_o^\top z_c) - 1\big)\, z_c.
$$

Reading: the term $-z_o$ (since $\sigma < 1$) *attracts* the context toward the center, each negative *repels* with a weight $\sigma(s_k) \in ]0,1[$ — strong if the negative is already too close.

Stochastic gradient descent: cost per pair $\mathcal{O}(K d)$, independent of $n$ — this is what made word2vec (and hence DeepWalk) scalable; the hierarchical softmax trick replaces the $\mathcal{O}(n)$ of the full softmax by $\mathcal{O}(\log n)$.
:::

::: prop
[Derivation 3.2 — node2vec: the biases $p$ and $q$ via transition probabilities]{.tag} At step $i$, the walk comes from $t$, is at $v$; for the candidate $x \in \mathcal{N}(v)$:
$$
\pi_{tx} = \frac{w_{tx}}{Z}\, \alpha_{pq}(t, x), \qquad \alpha_{pq}(t, x) = \begin{cases} 1/p & \text{if } d_{tx} = 0 \\ 1 & \text{if } d_{tx} = 1 \\ 1/q & \text{if } d_{tx} = 2 \end{cases}
$$
($d_{tx}$ = distance in the graph; $Z$ normalizes over $\mathcal{N}(v)$.)

In a simple graph, $d_{tx} \leq 2$ for every $x \in \mathcal{N}(v) \cup \{t\}$ if $t$ and $v$ are adjacent.

Three regimes:

-   **$p \lt 1$**: return toward $t$ favored — the walk stays in the close neighborhood (*BFS*): two nodes with analogous structural roles (hubs, bridges) get close embeddings — *structural equivalence*;
-   **$q \lt 1$**: vertices at $d_{tx} = 2$ are favored — the walk moves away (*DFS*): two nodes of the same community/cluster are close — *homophily*;
-   $p = q = 1$: uniform random walk — DeepWalk is a special case of node2vec.

The qualitative proof: with $p \to 0$, the probability of returning to $t$ dominates and the walk samples the 2-hop neighborhood of $t$ almost uniformly; with $q \to 0$, the chain avoids $t$ and behaves like a large-scale exploratory walk — find these behaviors again in exercise 2.
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 3.3 — NetMF: DeepWalk as matrix factorization (Qiu et al., 2018)]{.tag} As the window $b$ and the number of walks grow, DeepWalk converges to the (truncated, element-wise) factorization of the matrix:
$$
M = \log\Big( \frac{\mathrm{vol}(G)}{b\, T} \Big( \sum_{r=1}^{T} P^r \Big) D^{-1} \Big), \qquad \mathrm{vol}(G) = \sum_v d_v = 2m,
$$
that is, we look for $Z Z^\top \approx M$; $T$ plays the role of the effective horizon of the walks.

Consequences:

\(i\) a theoretical bridge — DeepWalk, LINE, PTE and node2vec are all factorizations of variants of $M$ (hence the name "NetMF", *Network Embedding as Matrix Factorization*);

\(ii\) a deterministic algorithm — factorizing $M$ directly (truncated SVD) matches or beats DeepWalk without drawing a single walk;

\(iii\) a diagnostic — the target matrix is built on $P = D^{-1}A$: the embeddings encode the *walks*, not the features, and remain *transductive* (a new node requires recomputing everything — direct motivation for the inductive GNNs of ch. 5).
:::

::: note
[The "word2vec on the graph" intuition — and its converse]{.tag} This is the historical NLP ↔ graphs bridge: a corpus of walks ≈ a corpus of sentences. DaSciM pushed the *reverse* idea — **Graph of Words** (ch. 11): representing a *document* by a graph of co-occurring terms and classifying it with graph tools. Both directions converge today in LLMs on graphs (ch. 10). To go beyond *walks* (with repetitions) toward *paths* (simple), see the Path Neural Networks (ch. 11; [Advanced GNN, ch. 2](../m2-advanced-gnn/index.html#ch2) and [ch. 9](../m2-advanced-gnn/index.html#ch9)).
:::

::: ex
[Example 3.4 — Karate Club: complete code]{.tag} Zachary's graph (34 nodes, 78 edges, 2 factions at the club split) is the "MNIST of graphs".

```python
import numpy as np, networkx as nx
from gensim.models import Word2Vec
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.metrics import normalized_mutual_info_score

G = nx.karate_club_graph()
y = np.array([0 if G.nodes[v]["club"] == "Mr. Hi" else 1 for v in G])

def biased_walk(G, v, p, q, length):
    walk, prev = [v], None
    for _ in range(length):
        cand = list(G.neighbors(walk[-1]))
        probs = []
        for x in cand:
            d = 0 if x == prev else nx.shortest_path_length(G, prev, x) if prev is not None else 1
            probs.append({0: 1/p, 1: 1.0, 2: 1/q}[d])
        probs = np.array(probs) / sum(probs)
        prev, nxt = walk[-1], np.random.choice(cand, p=probs)
        walk.append(nxt)
    return walk

walks = [ [str(u) for u in biased_walk(G, v, p=1, q=0.25, length=30)]
          for _ in range(80) for v in G.nodes() ]
model = Word2Vec(walks, vector_size=64, window=5, min_count=0, sg=1, epochs=10)
Z = np.array([model.wv[str(v)] for v in sorted(G.nodes())])
km = KMeans(n_clusters=2, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit(Z)
print("NMI :", normalized_mutual_info_score(y, km.labels_))   # ~0.5-0.8 depending on p, q, seed
```

Exercise 2: vary $(p, q)$ and relate the NMI to the BFS/DFS regime.
:::

## 4. Spectral filters and spectral clustering {#ch4}

To *filter* a signal carried by the nodes (smooth it, detect its sharp variations) or to *cut* a graph into communities, one needs a notion of frequency on a graph. The eigenvectors of the Laplacian (Definition 0.4) provide it; this chapter builds the graph Fourier transform, uses it for spectral clustering, then turns it into the first graph convolutions.

:::: def
[Definition 4.1 — Graph Fourier transform]{.tag} Let $L = U \Lambda U^\top$ (spectral decomposition, $U$ orthogonal, columns $u_1, \dots, u_n$). For a signal $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ carried by the nodes:

::: key
[Key result — graph Fourier transform]{.tag}
$$
\hat x = U^\top x \quad (\text{analysis}), \qquad x = U \hat x \quad (\text{synthesis}).
$$
:::

The "frequencies" are the eigenvalues $\lambda_k$ — small = slow variations over the graph (low frequencies), large = local alternations (high frequencies). This is the convolution of the Signal Processing module, with the Laplacian in place of $-i\frac{d}{dt}$: $L$ plays the role of the differential operator there.
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.2 — Variational characterization of $\lambda_2$ (Fiedler)]{.tag} For a connected graph:
$$
\lambda_2 \;=\; \min_{x \neq 0,\ x \perp \mathbf{1}} \frac{x^\top L x}{x^\top x},
$$
attained at the Fiedler vector $u_2$. The smaller $\lambda_2$, the more there exists a quasi-constant signal "almost orthogonal" to $\mathbf{1}$ — that is, two large blocks of weakly connected opposite values.

::: proof
Write $x = \sum_i c_i u_i$ (orthonormal basis); $x \perp \mathbf{1}$ forces $c_1 = 0$ since $u_1 = \mathbf{1}/\sqrt{n}$ (for a connected graph the kernel of $L$ is exactly spanned by $\mathbf{1}$ — the multiplicity computation of Definition 0.4).

Then $x^\top L x = \sum_{i \geq 2} \lambda_i c_i^2$ and $x^\top x = \sum_{i \geq 2} c_i^2$; the quotient is a weighted average of the $\lambda_i, i \geq 2$, hence lower-bounded by $\lambda_2$, with equality for $x = u_2$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 4.3 — Fiedler vector on two linked cliques (exact computation)]{.tag} Two $K_5$s ($\{u, x_1, \dots, x_4\}$ and $\{v, y_1, \dots, y_4\}$) linked by the bridge $(u, v)$. By symmetry, look for an antisymmetric eigenvector: $x_i = a$ on the 4 non-bridge nodes of the left, $u \mapsto b$, and opposite values on the right.

The equations $L x = \lambda x$ at a non-bridge node (degree 4) and at $u$ (degree 5) give:
$$
\lambda a = a - b \qquad \text{and} \qquad \lambda b = 6b - 4a \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; \lambda^2 - 7\lambda + 2 = 0.
$$
Hence
$$
\lambda_2 = \frac{7 - \sqrt{41}}{2} \approx 0.298, \qquad b = (1 - \lambda_2)\, a \approx 0.70\, a;
$$
the Fiedler vector equals, up to normalization:
$$
(\underbrace{1, 1, 1, 1}_{x_i}, \underbrace{0.70}_{u}, \underbrace{-0.70}_{v}, \underbrace{-1, -1, -1, -1}_{y_j})
$$
— the **sign exactly separates the two communities**, and the bridge node takes an intermediate value. This is *the* picture to remember about spectral clustering.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.4 — Spectral clustering: complete algorithm and justification (RatioCut relaxation)]{.tag} **Algorithm** (for $k$ communities):

1.  compute the first $k$ eigenvectors $u_1, \dots, u_k$ of $L$; form $F = [u_1 \| \dots \| u_k] \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times k}$;
2.  normalize each row of $F$;
3.  apply k-means to the $n$ rows of $F$ (spectral descriptor).

**Justification**: the RatioCut of a partition $\{C_1, \dots, C_k\}$ is
$$
\mathrm{RatioCut} = \sum_{j=1}^{k} \frac{\mathrm{cut}(C_j, \bar{C}_j)}{|C_j|}
$$
(cutting a small community is costly — unlike the plain minimization of the cut). Let $H \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times k}$ denote the renormalized indicators
$$
H_{ij} = \mathbb{1}[v_i \in C_j] / \sqrt{|C_j|}.
$$

::: proof
1.  *Exactness on the discrete class*. $H^\top H = I$ (orthogonal columns of norm 1). Moreover
    $$
    h_j^\top L h_j = \sum_{(u,v) \in E} (h_j(u) - h_j(v))^2 = \frac{1}{|C_j|} \times |\{(u,v) \in E : |\{u, v\} \cap C_j| = 1\}| = \frac{\mathrm{cut}(C_j, \bar{C_j})}{|C_j|}.
    $$
    So $\mathrm{tr}(H^\top L H) = \mathrm{RatioCut}$: minimizing RatioCut = minimizing $\mathrm{tr}(H^\top L H)$ over orthonormal *indicators*.
2.  *Relaxation*. We allow any $F \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times k}$ with $F^\top F = I$; the relaxed problem
    $$
    \min_{F^\top F = I} \mathrm{tr}(F^\top L F)
    $$
    has as solution the first $k$ eigenvectors (Ky Fan's theorem: shown by writing
    $$
    F^\top L F = \sum_{ij} (F^\top u_i)\,\lambda_i\,(u_j^\top F)
    $$
    and exchanging the order of summation, then minimizing the diagonalized coefficients).
3.  *Back to the discrete*. The rows of $F$ remain close to the rows of renormalized indicators; k-means groups them. [∎]{.qed}
:::

**Normalized Cut** variant (Shi & Malik): weighting by the volumes $d(C_j)$ leads to the generalized problem $L y = \lambda D y$, solved by the eigenvectors of $L_{\mathrm{sym}}$ — this is the version used in practice (and by scikit-learn).

Links: PCA (Machine Learning module — the matrix $F$ is the spectral counterpart of the projection); SBM (ch. 9) for the statistical approach; sign ambiguities of the eigenvectors — a real problem for GNNs, solved by SignNet ([Advanced GNN, ch. 4](../m2-advanced-gnn/index.html#ch4)).
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.5 — ChebNet: Chebyshev polynomials (Defferrard et al., 2016)]{.tag} Filtering exactly costs $y = U\, g_\theta(\Lambda)\, U^\top x$ — a full decomposition ($\mathcal{O}(n^3)$) *specific to each graph*.

Trick: take $g_\theta$ a **polynomial of degree $K$** in the Chebyshev basis. Set
$$
T_0(x) = 1, \qquad T_1(x) = x, \qquad T_{k+1}(x) = 2x T_k(x) - T_{k-1}(x),
$$
and $\tilde\Lambda = \frac{2\Lambda}{\lambda_{\max}} - I$ (rescaling to $[-1, 1]$); then
$$
y = \sum_{k=0}^K \theta_k\, T_k(\tilde L)\, x, \qquad \tilde L = \frac{2L}{\lambda_{\max}} - I,
$$
*without eigenvectors*: $K$-localized filter, weights $\theta$ *shared by all graphs*.

::: proof
1.  *Chebyshev recursion*. For $x = \cos\theta$, $T_k(x) = \cos(k\theta)$; the addition formula
    $$
    \cos((k{+}1)\theta) = 2\cos\theta \cos(k\theta) - \cos((k{-}1)\theta)
    $$
    gives the recursion (it propagates to all $x \in \mathbb{R}$ by polynomial identity).
2.  *Functional calculus*. Let us show $T_k(\tilde L) = U T_k(\tilde\Lambda) U^\top$: this is true for the monomials by recursion,
    $$
    \tilde L^m = (U \tilde\Lambda U^\top)^m = U \tilde\Lambda^m U^\top,
    $$
    the inner products $U^\top U$ canceling — hence for every polynomial. Thus
    $$
    y = U\, g_\theta(\tilde\Lambda)\, U^\top x = g_\theta(\tilde L)\, x:
    $$
    the spectral filter is expressed as a polynomial of $L$ applied directly to $x$.
3.  *Locality*. $\tilde L x$ at a node only combines $x_v$ and $\{x_u : u \in \mathcal{N}(v)\}$.

    By recursion on the Chebyshev recursion (linear combination of $\tilde L^k x$, $k \leq K$), the output at $v$ depends only on the $K$-neighborhood. [∎]{.qed}
:::

Cost: $\mathcal{O}(K |E|)$ per application — linear in the size of the graph.
::::

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.6 — From spectral to spatial: the equality demonstrated]{.tag} Every filter that is a *polynomial of degree $K$* in $L$ is exactly a $K$-localized operator, and conversely every message passing operator with $K$ layers whose propagation is a polynomial of $A$ realizes a polynomial spectral filter.

::: proof
Forward direction: developed in (iii) above.

Conversely: a local layer
$$
y_v = \sum_{u \in \{v\} \cup \mathcal{N}(v)} c_{uv} x_u
$$
with uniform weights by symmetry writes in matrix form $y = \sum_{k \leq 1} c_k\, \Pi_k(A) x$ for polynomials $\Pi_k$ of degree $\leq 1$ (the diagonal term is $\Pi_0$, the edges $\Pi_1$).

Composing $K$ layers without non-linearity, $y = \Pi(A) x$ with $\deg \Pi \leq K$.

Since $L = D - A$ is itself a polynomial in $A$ (with $D$ fixed by the graph), $\Pi(A) = g(L)$ for a polynomial $g$ of the same degree.

The non-linearities between layers break the exact equality — this is precisely the gap between the spectral "CNN on graph" and the spatial GNN: the GNN generalizes the filter by inserting point-wise non-linearities, like a 1D CNN. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

## 5. GNNs and message passing {#ch5}

Spectral filters are tied to the eigenvectors of one fixed graph. We want instead a layer that applies to any graph, costs time linear in the number of edges and trains like an ordinary network layer; message passing is that layer — each node updates its vector from the vectors of its neighbors.

::: def
[Definition 5.1 — The message passing layer (MPNN, Gilmer et al., 2017)]{.tag}
$$
h_v^{(\ell+1)} = \phi\Big(h_v^{(\ell)},\ \underset{u \in \mathcal{N}(v)}{\mathrm{AGG}}\ \big\{\psi\big(h_v^{(\ell)}, h_u^{(\ell)}\big)\big\}\Big)
$$
**message** $\psi$ (computed by the neighbor), **aggregation** $\mathrm{AGG}$ (permutation-invariant: sum, mean, max, attention), **update** $\phi$.

One layer = one round of message passing = one convolution = one diffusion step on the graph. The choice of $\mathrm{AGG}$ is not innocent: mean/max lose cardinality ({a, a} and {a} have the same mean and the same max); this is the subject of the GIN theorem ([Advanced GNN, ch. 2](../m2-advanced-gnn/index.html#ch2)).
:::

:::: thm
[Derivation 5.2 — GCN from spectral convolution (Kipf & Welling, 2017)]{.tag} Start from the Chebyshev filter of Theorem 4.5 truncated at $K = 1$, on the normalized Laplacian $L_{\mathrm{sym}} = I - D^{-1/2} A D^{-1/2}$, whose eigenvalues lie in $[0, 2]$.

1.  Approximating $\lambda_{\max} \approx 2$ gives $\tilde L = L_{\mathrm{sym}} - I$, hence
    $$
    g_\theta(L)\, x \approx \theta_0\, x + \theta_1 (L_{\mathrm{sym}} - I)\, x = \theta_0\, x - \theta_1\, D^{-1/2} A D^{-1/2}\, x.
    $$
2.  Keeping a single parameter $\theta = \theta_0 = -\theta_1$ (fewer parameters, less overfitting on small graphs):
    $$
    g_\theta(L)\, x \approx \theta\,\big(I + D^{-1/2} A D^{-1/2}\big)\, x.
    $$
3.  The operator $I + D^{-1/2} A D^{-1/2}$ has its eigenvalues in $[0, 2]$: applied $\ell$ times it can multiply some components by up to $2^\ell$, and deep stacks become numerically unstable.
4.  The **renormalization trick** replaces it by $\tilde D^{-1/2} \tilde A \tilde D^{-1/2}$, where $\tilde A = A + I$ adds a self-loop to each node and $\tilde D$ is the degree matrix of $\tilde A$; its eigenvalues lie in $(-1, 1]$.

Adding the features $X$, a weight matrix and a non-linearity, we obtain the GCN layer:

::: key
[Key result — the GCN layer]{.tag}
$$
H^{(\ell+1)} = \sigma\Big(\tilde D^{-1/2}\, \tilde A\, \tilde D^{-1/2}\, H^{(\ell)}\, W^{(\ell)}\Big), \qquad H^{(0)} = X,
$$
:::

a degree-normalized mean of the transformed representations of the node and of its neighbors; $L$ layers give a receptive field of $L$ hops.

Because the gains of the propagator stay in $(-1, 1]$, depth no longer makes the signal explode — but repeated averaging makes it collapse instead: this is the over-smoothing of Theorem 5.3.
::::

::: thm
[GraphSAGE (Hamilton et al., 2017) — algorithm and pseudo-code]{.tag} For each node, aggregate a *sample* of neighbors then concatenate with the current representation:

```python
input : G, features X, depth K, sample sizes s_1..s_K
for v in V : h_v^(0) = x_v
for l = 1 .. K :
    for v in V :
        S_v = uniform sample of N(v) of size s_l               # K neighbors in the paper
        a_v^(l) = AGG({ h_u^(l-1) : u in S_v })                 # mean / LSTM / pool
        h_v^(l) = sigma( W_l . [ h_v^(l-1) || a_v^(l) ] )       # concatenation!
        h_v^(l) = h_v^(l) / ||h_v^(l)||                          # L2 normalization
output : z_v = h_v^(K)
```

The **concatenation** preserves the information specific to the node (otherwise the mean of the neighbors crushes the local signal); the **fixed per-layer sampling** bounds the minibatch (ch. 7); the whole scheme is *inductive*: the weights $W_l$ are re-applied to unseen nodes/graphs.

Special cases: AGG = mean ≈ GCN without renormalization; AGG = pool (MLP + max); AGG = LSTM over neighbors *randomly ordered* (the ordering breaks invariance… an accepted approximation; the ordering problem is addressed by GOAT, ch. 11).
:::

::: thm
[GAT (Veličković et al., 2018) — equations and complexity]{.tag} Edge weights *learned by attention*:
$$
e_{uv} = \mathrm{LeakyReLU}\big(a^\top [\,W h_u \| W h_v\,]\big), \qquad \alpha_{uv} = \frac{\exp(e_{uv})}{\sum_{u' \in \mathcal{N}(v)} \exp(e_{u'v})}, \qquad h_v^{(\ell+1)} = \sigma\Big(\sum_{u \in \mathcal{N}(v)} \alpha_{uv}\, W h_u^{(\ell)}\Big)
$$
with $T$ parallel attention heads (T projections $W^{(t)}$) concatenated or averaged.

Per-layer complexity, with $F$ and $F'$ the input and output dimensions: $\mathcal{O}(|V| F F' + |E| F')$ — *linear* in edges, comparable to GCN, but with weights *tailored to each edge*: useful when the graph is noisy or some relations matter more (suspicious transactions!).

Structurally identical to the attention of transformers (Deep Learning module): here the attention mask is *given* by the graph, there it is *computed* — the graph transformers of [Advanced GNN, ch. 5](../m2-advanced-gnn/index.html#ch5) close the loop by learning the attention *and* biasing it with structure.
:::

::: note
[Beyond the homogeneous graph: R-GCN, edge features]{.tag}

-   **R-GCN** (Schlichtkrull et al., 2018): *relational* graph (edge types $r$ in $\mathcal{R}$);
    $$
    h_v^{(\ell+1)} = \sigma\big(W_0 h_v^{(\ell)} + \sum_{r \in \mathcal{R}} \sum_{u \in \mathcal{N}_r(v)} \frac{1}{c_{v,r}} W_r\, h_u^{(\ell)}\big).
    $$
    To avoid the parameter explosion ($|\mathcal{R}| \times F \times F'$): *basis* decomposition $W_r = \sum_b a_{rb} V_b$ or *block-diagonal*. Typical use: encoding knowledge graphs for link prediction (ch. 6).
-   **Edge features**: (a) line graph (each edge becomes a node); (b) convolution over edges (NNConv): $\psi(h_u, e_{uv})$ instead of $\psi(h_u)$ — the chemical bond carries a type; (c) conditioned attention (GAT can inject $e_{uv}$ into the $e_{uv}$-score).
-   **Hierarchical pooling**: DiffPool (Ying et al., 2018) learns a soft assignment matrix
    $$
    S^{(\ell)} = \mathrm{softmax}(\mathrm{GNN}_A(H^{(\ell)}))
    $$
    and contracts the graph: $H^{(\ell+1)} = S^{(\ell)\top} H^{(\ell)}$, $A^{(\ell+1)} = S^{(\ell)\top} A^{(\ell)} S^{(\ell)}$ — neural coarse-graining, costly but hierarchical; alternatives: sort/TopK pooling, pyramidal readout.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.3 — Over-smoothing: proof on a regular graph]{.tag} On a connected $d$-regular graph, GCN propagation without weights/non-linearity satisfies $H^{(\ell)} = P^\ell X$ with $P = \frac{A + I}{d + 1}$. Then
$$
H^{(\ell)} \xrightarrow[\ell \to \infty]{} \frac{\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top}{n}\, X,
$$
the *harmonic solution* (global mean), at geometric rate $\rho^\ell$ with
$$
\rho = \max_{i \geq 2} \frac{|\lambda_i(A) + 1|}{d + 1} < 1.
$$

::: proof
On a $d$-regular graph, $\tilde D = (d+1)I$, hence $\tilde D^{-1/2} \tilde A \tilde D^{-1/2} = (A + I)/(d+1) =: P$.

Since $A$ is real symmetric, write $X$ in its eigenbasis:
$$
A = \sum_i \lambda_i u_i u_i^\top,
$$
with $u_1 = \mathbf{1}/\sqrt{n}$, $\lambda_1 = d > \lambda_2 \geq \dots$, and $\lambda_i < d$ for $i \geq 2$ (equality only if there is a distinct connected component). Then
$$
P^\ell = \sum_i \big(\frac{\lambda_i + 1}{d+1}\big)^\ell u_i u_i^\top .
$$

The $i = 1$ term equals exactly $\frac{\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top}{n}$; all the others have a ratio $\frac{\lambda_i + 1}{d + 1}$ in $\big[\frac{1-d}{d+1}, 1\big)$ (since $-d \leq \lambda_i < d$), hence of absolute value $< 1$, and decay geometrically.

All the information of the non-constant components is erased: every node converges to the same mean row vector — the embeddings collapse. [∎]{.qed}
:::

With weights and non-linearities, the phenomenon persists (rank collapse; Oono & Suzuki, ICLR 2020): this is a *structural* limit of GCN depth. Remedies:

-   **Jumping Knowledge** (Xu et al., 2018): the readout aggregates *all* the depths
    $$
    h_v = \mathrm{JK}(h_v^{(1)}, \dots, h_v^{(L)})
    $$
    (concat / max / LSTM-attention): each node chooses its scale;
-   residuals and normalizations (GCNII, APPNP — developed in [Advanced GNN, ch. 3](../m2-advanced-gnn/index.html#ch3));
-   in practice, 2-4 layers usually suffice: the useful depth is the range of the statistical dependence of the task.

A second structural limit — *over-squashing* (topological bottlenecks) — is different: it concerns the *channel* rather than the representation, and is addressed by *rewiring*; the whole topic is in [Advanced GNN, ch. 3](../m2-advanced-gnn/index.html#ch3). A third limit: expressivity bounded by 1-WL ([Advanced GNN, ch. 2](../m2-advanced-gnn/index.html#ch2)).
::::

### Heterophily: when neighbors differ

The seventh lecture of the official programme treats heterophily and temporal graphs. GCN-style averaging implicitly assumes *homophily* — linked nodes tend to share their label. Fraud rings (fraudsters link to honest accounts they exploit), dating networks, protein interactions or the "is a student of" relation violate it.

::: def
[Definition 5.4 — Homophily ratio]{.tag} For a labeled graph, the **edge homophily** is
$$
h = \frac{|\{(u,v) \in E : y_u = y_v\}|}{|E|} \in [0, 1].
$$

Citation graphs are strongly homophilous (Cora $h \approx 0.81$, Citeseer $\approx 0.74$). The standard heterophilous benchmarks are far lower (Texas $\approx 0.11$, Wisconsin $\approx 0.21$, Chameleon $\approx 0.23$, Squirrel $\approx 0.22$; Pei et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2020).

A low $h$ is not harmful in itself: what matters is whether the label distribution of a node's neighbors is *informative* about its own label (Ma et al., 2022).
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 5.5 — Mean aggregation on a perfectly heterophilous graph, computed]{.tag} Take a connected $d$-regular bipartite graph whose two sides are the two classes, with a scalar feature $x_v = +1$ on one side and $-1$ on the other ($h = 0$). One GCN propagation (Theorem 5.3, $P = (A + I)/(d+1)$) gives
$$
(Px)_v = \frac{x_v + \sum_{u \in \mathcal{N}(v)} x_u}{d + 1} = \frac{1 - d}{d + 1}\, x_v.
$$

For $d = 1$ the signal is erased; for $d = 3$ it becomes $-0.5\,x_v$: sign flipped, magnitude halved; with $L$ layers it shrinks as $\big(\frac{d-1}{d+1}\big)^L$.

Spectral reading (Definition 0.4): this label signal has
$$
x^\top L x = \sum_{(u,v) \in E}(x_u - x_v)^2 = 4m,
$$
the largest possible value for $\pm 1$ signals — it is a *high-frequency* signal, and GCN propagation is a *low-pass* filter (ch. 4) that attenuates exactly such components.

Mixing the node with its neighbors inside one average makes the two cancel; keeping them separate,
$$
h_v = W_1 x_v \,\|\, W_2\, \mathrm{mean}_{u \in \mathcal{N}(v)} x_u, \quad \text{here } (x_v, -x_v),
$$
preserves the information fully.
:::

::: note
[Architectures for heterophily]{.tag} **H2GCN** (Zhu et al., 2020) combines three designs: ego/neighbor separation (as above, and as in GraphSAGE's concatenation), aggregation over 2-hop neighborhoods (in a bipartite graph the same class sits two hops away) and combination of all intermediate layers (as Jumping Knowledge).

**GPR-GNN** (Chien et al., 2021) learns the coefficients $\gamma_k$ of a polynomial filter $\sum_k \gamma_k P^k X$; negative coefficients produce *high-pass* filters (Proposition 4.6 makes this a spectral design).

**FAGCN** uses signed attention weights, letting a node subtract the messages of dissimilar neighbors. The interaction of heterophily with over-smoothing and over-squashing is developed in [Advanced GNN, ch. 3](../m2-advanced-gnn/index.html#ch3).
:::

### Temporal graphs

::: def
[Definition 5.6 — Discrete- and continuous-time dynamic graphs]{.tag} A **discrete-time dynamic graph** is a sequence of snapshots $G_1, \dots, G_T$ (one per day, per week); a **continuous-time dynamic graph** is a stream of timestamped events $(u, v, t, e_{uv})$ — transactions, messages, citations.

Tasks: *temporal link prediction* (will $u$ interact with $v$ at time $t$?), *dynamic node classification* (is this account fraudulent now?), and forecasting node signals on a fixed graph (traffic: spatio-temporal graphs).

The causality rule: a prediction at time $t$ may use only events with timestamps $< t$.
:::

::: thm
[Models 5.7 — Snapshot models, TGAT and TGN]{.tag} **Snapshot models** run a GNN on each $G_\tau$ and an RNN over time, either on the node embeddings (GCRN) or on the GNN weights themselves (EvolveGCN, Pareja et al., 2020).

**TGAT** (Xu et al., 2020) handles continuous time with a GAT-like attention over a node's *past* neighbors, each message concatenated with a functional time encoding of the elapsed time $\Delta t$:
$$
\Phi(\Delta t) = \big[\cos(\omega_1 \Delta t + b_1), \dots, \cos(\omega_k \Delta t + b_k)\big],
$$
with learned frequencies — a random-feature form of a translation-invariant kernel in time (Bochner's theorem).

**TGN** (Rossi et al., 2020) adds a *memory* $s_v(t)$ per node, updated at each event involving $v$ by a recurrent cell,
$$
s_v(t) \leftarrow \mathrm{GRU}\big(s_v(t^-),\ \mathrm{msg}(s_v(t^-), s_u(t^-), \Delta t, e_{uv})\big);
$$
embeddings are computed by temporal attention over recent neighbors and their memories, and an MLP decodes link probabilities.

Events are processed in chronological batches, and the memory is updated *after* the batch has been predicted, so that no event informs its own prediction.
:::

::: ex
[Example 5.8 — Temporal neighborhoods and leakage, computed]{.tag} Events:
$$
(a, b, 1), \quad (b, c, 2), \quad (a, c, 5), \quad (c, d, 7).
$$
Query at $t = 6$: will $c$ interact with $d$?

The admissible history is the first three events. The temporal neighbors of $c$ are $b$ (elapsed $\Delta t = 4$) and $a$ ($\Delta t = 1$).

Their time encodings $\Phi(4)$ and $\Phi(1)$ differ, so the attention can favour the recent contact.

Node $d$ has no past event: the prediction is *inductive* and rests on its features and on the time encoding only.

A static GNN trained on the aggregated graph would contain the edge $(c, d)$ — the very event to be predicted — and report an inflated score; the honest protocol splits events chronologically (train on $t \leq 5$, test on $t > 5$), as in Example 8.1. Memory-based models and temporal benchmarks are developed in [Advanced GNN, ch. 6](../m2-advanced-gnn/index.html#ch6).
:::

```python
import torch
from torch_geometric.nn import GCNConv, GATConv
from torch_geometric.datasets import Planetoid

dataset = Planetoid(root="/tmp/Cora", name="Cora")   # 2708 nodes, 5429 edges, 7 classes
data = dataset[0]

class GCN(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_in, d_hid, n_classes):
        super().__init__()
        self.c1, self.c2 = GCNConv(d_in, d_hid), GCNConv(d_hid, n_classes)
    def forward(self, x, edge_index):
        return self.c2(torch.relu(self.c1(x, edge_index)), edge_index)

model = GCN(dataset.num_features, 64, dataset.num_classes)
opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=0.01, weight_decay=5e-4)
for epoch in range(200):
    opt.zero_grad()
    out = model(data.x, data.edge_index)
    loss = torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy(out[data.train_mask], data.y[data.train_mask])
    loss.backward(); opt.step()
acc = (model(data.x, data.edge_index).argmax(1)[data.test_mask]
       == data.y[data.test_mask]).float().mean()
print(f"Cora test accuracy : {acc:.3f}")   # ~0.81 with this simple setting
```

## 6. Link prediction and graph auto-encoders {#ch6}

Many graphs are incomplete: a recommender wants the purchases that have not happened yet, a knowledge graph misses true facts. This chapter turns the node representations of ch. 3 and 5 into scores for *pairs* of nodes, and trains them to recover the missing edges.

::: def
[Definition 6.1 — Link prediction]{.tag} Predicting the existence (or the type) of a missing edge $(u, v)$: the most widespread task in industry — recommendation ("who will like what?"), completion of knowledge graphs ("does this drug target this protein?"), prediction of future interactions ([Advanced GNN, ch. 6](../m2-advanced-gnn/index.html#ch6) for the temporal case).

Protocol: mask a fraction of the edges (10%), sample as many "negatives" (non-adjacent pairs), score all the pairs, measure AUC / Hits@k.
:::

:::: thm
[GAE / VGAE (Kipf & Welling, 2016) — graph auto-encoders]{.tag} **GAE**: encoder $Z = \mathrm{GCN}(X, A)$; decode by dot product — the reconstruction probability of an edge:

::: key
[Key result — the GAE decoder]{.tag}
$$
p(A_{uv} = 1 \mid z_u, z_v) = \sigma(z_u^\top z_v).
$$
:::

Training: maximize the likelihood of the observed edges *and* minimize that of the negatives — the cross-entropy of the negative sampling of ch. 3, transposed:
$$
\mathcal{L} = -\sum_{(u,v) \in E^+} \log \sigma(z_u^\top z_v) \; - \sum_{(u,v') \in E^-} \log \big(1 - \sigma(z_u^\top z_{v'})\big).
$$

**VGAE**: variational Gaussian encoder
$$
q(Z \mid X, A) = \prod_i \mathcal{N}(z_i;\ \mu_i, \mathrm{diag}(\sigma_i^2))
$$
with $\mu = \mathrm{GCN}_\mu(X, A)$, $\log\sigma = \mathrm{GCN}_\sigma(X, A)$, prior $\mathcal{N}(0, I)$; one maximizes the ELBO:
$$
\mathcal{L} = \mathbb{E}_{q}[\log p(A \mid Z)] - \mathrm{KL}\big(q(Z \mid X,A)\,\|\,\mathcal{N}(0, I)\big),
$$
reparameterization $z_i = \mu_i + \sigma_i \odot \varepsilon$, $\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$.

Recap in two lines. The ELBO is a lower bound on $\log p(A)$, tight when $q$ equals the posterior $p(Z \mid A)$: the bound behind EM in [Machine Learning, ch. 7](../m1p1-machine-learning/index.html#ch7). Writing $z_i$ as a differentiable function of $\mu_i$, $\sigma_i$ and an independent noise lets backpropagation train both GCNs on a Monte Carlo estimate of the ELBO. Both ideas are taught in full in [Deep Learning, ch. 9](../m1p1-deep-learning/index.html#ch9) and [Deep Learning P2, 7.3](../m1p2-deep-learning-p2/index.html#dl-generative); on the P2 path, 7.3 comes after this session.

Results: on Cora, AUC $\approx 0.91$ (GAE) and $\approx 0.92$ (VGAE) — the prior regularizes the dot product (cf. the connection with SBM inference, ch. 9).
::::

::: note
[Scoring pairs: the choice of the decision function]{.tag}

-   **dot product** $z_u^\top z_v$ — rank-$d$ decomposition, symmetric, related to NetMF (ch. 3);
-   **MLP over $(z_u \odot z_v, z_u - z_v)$** or concatenation — asymmetric (important in recommendation: "A buys B" ≠ "B buys A");
-   **relational distances** (KGC, below);
-   **negatives**: uniform (easy) vs hard — pairs sharing a neighbor (popularity-biased); the choice of negatives changes the learned ranking (Deep Learning module, contrastive; NLP module for the word2vec analogy).
:::

::: thm
[PinSage (Ying et al., 2018) — recommendation at industrial scale]{.tag} The Pinterest deployment of GraphSAGE: a user-pin graph of **3 billion nodes and 18 billion edges**, trained by minibatches. Two key differences from GraphSAGE:

1.  **importance sampling**: instead of uniform neighbors, the $T$ neighbors most often visited by short random walks started at the node (a personalized PageRank score); their normalized visit counts also weight the aggregation;
2.  **ranking loss** (hinge margin): $\max(0, m - s(u, v^+) + s(u, v^-_h))$ with $v^-_h$ a *hard negative* (a pin popular but not clicked); production requires candidates ranked by approximate score, that is approximate nearest-neighbour vector search, taught in [Large Language Models, ch. 7](../m2-large-language-models/index.html#ch7) (M2).

LLGA lesson: at this scale, the architecture matters less than the *system* (sampling, cache, GPU) — this is the bridge to ch. 7.
:::

::: note
[Knowledge graph completion (KGC)]{.tag} Link prediction on a typed heterogeneous graph (heads $h$, relations $r$, tails $t$):

-   **TransE** (Bordes et al., 2013): embeddings in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with the energy score $f(h, r, t) = -\|h + r - t\|$ — the relation is a *translation*; margin-based training (positives vs corrupted negatives); illuminating but limited (1-N, symmetric relations);
-   **R-GCN + score** (ch. 5): the encoder propagates over the typed graph, a decoder (DistMult: $\langle h, \mathrm{diag}(r), t \rangle$) scores the triples — the "encode-decode" architecture dominates;
-   **GraphRAG link**: an enterprise KG completed by KGC becomes queryable by an LLM (ch. 10); the completion deficits guide the collection of data — a data/model loop specific to the LLGA trade.
:::

## 7. GNNs at scale {#ch7}

The models of ch. 5 were trained on Cora, which fits in memory; industrial graphs have millions of nodes and billions of edges. This chapter explains why full-batch training breaks at that scale and presents the three standard ways of training on pieces of the graph.

::: def
[Why full-batch does not fit]{.tag} The gradient of a GCN layer mobilizes *the whole* graph: activation memory $\mathcal{O}((|V| + |E|) d)$ per layer, not to mention the densification of the deep layers.

On ogbn-products (2.4 million nodes, 61.9 million edges), the full-batch does not fit on a GPU; three families of solutions, all grounded on the same observation: the dependence of a node over $L$ layers is limited to its $L$-neighborhood.
:::

::: thm
[7.1 — Neighborhood minibatching (GraphSAGE / NeighborSampler)]{.tag} For a batch of target nodes $\mathcal{B}$ and a depth $L$ with sampling sizes $(s_L, \dots, s_1)$ (fanouts):

```python
N_L = B                                             # the target nodes of the batch
for l = L .. 1 :                                    # from the output layer down to the input
    N_{l-1} = N_l + (s_l sampled neighbors of each node of N_l)
compute h^(1), ..., h^(L) layer by layer, layer l only on the nodes of N_l
update the parameters with the loss on the outputs of B only
```

Subgraph size: $|\mathcal{B}| \times (1 + s_L (1 + s_{L-1}(\dots)))$. With $L = 2$, $s_1 = s_2 = 10$, a batch of 1 node touches at most $1 + 10 + 100 = 111$ nodes — *bounded, independent of $n$*.

Two subtleties: (i) the estimator is *unbiased in expectation* for the mean over neighbors, but the variance explodes at the hubs (hence decreasing fanouts); (ii) the nested samplings create redundant computation across batches (the "expansive neighborhood"; PyG's NeighborLoader implements exactly this).
:::

::: thm
[7.2 — Cluster-GCN (Chiang et al., 2019): partitioning]{.tag} Partition the graph into $k$ clusters (METIS), each batch = one *whole cluster*: GCN training on the induced subgraph costs $\mathcal{O}(|E_c| d + |V_c| d^2)$ and each full epoch costs $\mathcal{O}(|E|)$ — like the full-batch, but in constant memory, and deep GCNs become trainable again.

The price: the partition bias — the edges between clusters are invisible during the step.

The correction of the paper builds each batch from *several* clusters drawn at random, which restores the edges between the chosen clusters and varies the batches from one epoch to the next; for deep models it also enlarges the diagonal of the normalized adjacency, $\bar A = \tilde A + \lambda\,\mathrm{diag}(\tilde A)$, so that each node keeps weight on its own representation.

Even better: link the clusters by a "virtual graph" of clusters — a precursor of the GraphRAG hierarchies (ch. 10).
:::

::: thm
[7.3 — GraphSAINT (Zeng et al., 2020): sampling subgraphs, unbiasedly]{.tag} Flip the perspective: first sample a subgraph $\mathcal{G}_s$ (by nodes, by edges, or by random walks), then compute a *corrected* gradient on it.

The key is the **normalization by inclusion probabilities**. Let $p_v$ be the probability that the sampler includes node $v$ and $p_{uv}$ the probability that it includes edge $(u, v)$ (both estimated once, by pre-sampling).

Inside the subgraph, the message from $u$ to $v$ is divided by $\alpha_{uv} = p_{uv}/p_v$, which makes each aggregation an unbiased estimator of the full-graph aggregation, and the loss is reweighted as
$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{batch}} = \sum_{v \in \mathcal{G}_s} \frac{\mathcal{L}_v}{\lambda_v}, \qquad \lambda_v = |V|\, p_v,
$$
whose expectation is exactly the mean loss over all the nodes:
$$
\mathbb{E}\big[\sum_{v \in \mathcal{G}_s} \mathcal{L}_v / \lambda_v\big] = \sum_{v \in V} p_v \mathcal{L}_v / (|V| p_v).
$$
The paper proves both statements by writing the expectation over the sampling scheme.

Hidden benefit: the batches are "dense" (no expansive neighborhood), and walk-based sampling captures the community structure.

The general picture: *bias-variance-memory* — neighbor-sampling (high variance, zero bias); cluster-GCN (partition bias, zero variance); GraphSAINT (unbiased by reweighting, variance controlled by RW sampling).

These trade-offs are the daily bread of [Advanced GNN, ch. 1](../m2-advanced-gnn/index.html#ch1) (and of the Emerging ML module for the federated parallel: partitions = clients).
:::

::: note
[OGB — measuring honestly at scale (Hu et al., 2020)]{.tag}

  Benchmark               Size                              Task
  ----------------------- --------------------------------- ----------------------
  ogbn-arxiv              169,343 nodes, 1.2M edges         node classification
  ogbn-products           2.4M nodes, 61.9M edges           node classification
  ogbg-molhiv / molpcba   41,127 / 437k molecules           graph classification
  ogbl-ppa / citation2    large bipartite/citation graphs   link prediction

Rules of the game: fixed splits, defined model selection protocols, public leaderboards — the experimental hygiene of [Advanced GNN, ch. 1](../m2-advanced-gnn/index.html#ch1) (Dwivedi et al., "Benchmarking GNNs") is not optional: at this scale, progress is measured in tenths of a point and only strict protocols distinguish it from noise.
:::

## 8. Applications and hands-on {#ch8}

The previous chapters gave the models; this chapter maps them onto the use cases met in industry, then gives the protocol of a first honest experiment — the step where most graph projects go wrong.

-   **Recommendation**: user-item graph, link prediction (ch. 6); PinSage (3B nodes, 18B edges) = GraphSAGE at industrial scale; cold-start = the inductive case par excellence;
-   **Fraud detection**: node classification on the transaction graph; typical signals: counter proximities, money-laundering cycles (the *motifs* matter!), card hubs — GNNs capture the multihop neighborhood that an iid model ignores; public data: the Elliptic Bitcoin transaction graph (Exercise 16); temporal version in [Advanced GNN, ch. 6](../m2-advanced-gnn/index.html#ch6);
-   **Chemistry / biotech**: molecule = graph (atoms = nodes, bonds = edges); graph classification to predict properties (toxicity, solubility, HIV activity); benchmarks: ZINC, QM9, ogbg-mol\*; 3D geometry and equivariance: Definition 8.2 below, developed in [Advanced GNN, ch. 8](../m2-advanced-gnn/index.html#ch8) and [Analysis and Deep Learning on Geometric Data, ch. 7](../m2-geometric-deep-learning/index.html#ch7);
-   **Knowledge graph completion**: link prediction on heterogeneous KGs (TransE, R-GCN — ch. 6); the basis of "enterprise" RAG (ch. 10);
-   **Scale up**: neighborhood minibatching, clustering, sampling (ch. 7), multi-node GPUs ([Advanced GNN, ch. 1](../m2-advanced-gnn/index.html#ch1)); open benchmarks: OGB.

::: note
[Architecture choice — quick decision sheet]{.tag} 

-   Homogeneous graph, rich features: GCN (baseline);
-   noisy/heterogeneous edges (fraud): GAT / R-GCN;
-   inductive production: GraphSAGE;
-   need to distinguish local structures (cycles): GIN + motif features ([Advanced GNN, ch. 2](../m2-advanced-gnn/index.html#ch2));
-   long-range dependencies (molecules, QA over KGs): graph transformer ([Advanced GNN, ch. 5](../m2-advanced-gnn/index.html#ch5)).

Always: 2-4 layers, skip connections, light dropedge as a first choice.
:::

::: ex
[Example 8.1 — Hands-on: evaluating link prediction without leakage]{.tag} Take a graph with 10,000 edges and the task "predict the missing edges". The tempting protocol trains a GAE (ch. 6) on all the edges, then scores 1,000 of them as "test" edges.

The encoder has already passed messages *along* those edges, so their endpoints have similar embeddings by construction, and the AUC is optimistic. The honest protocol has three steps.

1.  **Split before training.** Remove 1,000 test edges (10%) and 500 validation edges (5%) from the graph, and draw as many non-adjacent pairs as negatives for each set.
2.  **Train on what remains.** The encoder sees only the 8,500 training edges, both as supervision and as the graph along which messages are passed; node features computed from the structure (degrees, PageRank) are computed on this training graph too.
3.  **Score the held-out pairs.** Report the AUC (or Hits@k) of the test positives against the test negatives, after choosing the hyperparameters on the validation set only.
